place.en: The Si · Before the stone door

setup.zh: 冬月初一，泗水退潮，秘境开门。领了灵石，往前十步，照旧是那只描金小木匣。马小宝眼皮也不抬：「沈小满。两块。」
setup.en: The first of the eleventh month: the Si ebbs and the hidden realm opens. Stones drawn, ten steps on, the same little gilt box. Ma Xiaobao doesn't lift his eyelids: "Shen Xiaoman. Two."

recap.zh: 冬月初一，沉鼎秘境开了。阿禾把她背熟了的地图借给你：「五十文，记着。」
recap.en: The first of the eleventh month, the Chending hidden realm opened. A He lent you the map she'd learned by heart: "Fifty cash. On account."

en: The first of the eleventh month; the Si ebbs.

story.zh:
十月的最后一夜，三更刚过，沉鼎观外门男弟子的大通铺上，靠窗的一个人忽然坐了起来，叫道：「水没了！」

这一声又尖又急，满屋子的人给他叫醒了一大半，有人骂娘，有人摸鞋，有人一脚踩在旁人脸上。小满睡在最靠门的铺上，披着被子挤到窗前，往山下一望，登时呆了。月亮底下，泗水不见了。平日里宽宽的一条河，缩成了河心一道亮线，两边是一眼望不到头的淤泥滩，泥上泛着白光；沉鼎山脚下那一段河湾里，泥滩上立着一样黑黢黢的东西，方方正正，一丈多高，像一扇门。

「秘境。」叫醒众人的那个人道，声音都在抖，「秘境开了。」告示栏上贴了一两天的那张纸，写的是冬月初一；谁也没想到，那条河是在半夜里，一口气没的。

小满躺回铺上，摸着胸口的木牌，小声道：「银月，左边那道崖，你知道么？」木牌没有回答。通铺那一头，靠火盆那张最好的铺上，「咯吱、咯吱」，一下一下，很慢，很匀，马小宝又在嚼桂花糕了。嚼完了，他把油纸团一团，往后一扔，扔在最边上那张铺上，含含糊糊地冲着黑地里道：「怕什么。崖上掉下去的，都是傻子。」没有人接他的话。

最边上那张铺挨着漏风的窗户，睡的是个瘦长的老弟子，人都叫他老蔫。他是马家佃户的儿子，进门三年，练气二层，一天说不上三句话。他把那团油纸捡起来，展平了，叠成方方的一块，揣进怀里，预备第二天一早替马小宝扔。十月十二那天夜里，柴房里打到第二十下，五个人里缩回手、低低说了一句「够了」的，便是他。从那以后，马小宝便叫他睡窗户底下。

冬月初一，天还没亮，外门执事房门口照例排起了长龙。周衡坐在榆木桌子后面，面前摊着那本厚得能当枕头的账簿，叫一个名字，发三块灵石，再从脚边一只旧木箱里摸出一块铜名牌，背面刻着那人的名字。他今日的神色和往常不大一样，发一个，便要抬起头来叮嘱一句：「秘境里头，保命要紧。灵草丢了，明年还长；人丢了，账上不好记。」有个新来的弟子问他：「周师兄，秘境里死过人么？」周衡翻了翻账簿，翻到最后几页，那几页的纸比别的黄，上面记着几个名字，名字底下画着一道红杠。他看了一会儿，把账簿合上了，道：「保命要紧。」

排在小满后头的，正是老蔫。他领了三块灵石，却不走，盯着那本合上的账簿，低声问了一句：「周师兄，画了红杠的……家里知道么？」周衡抬起眼来看了他一眼：「观里派人去说。」老蔫点点头，把三块灵石揣进怀里，跟那团叠得方方的油纸揣在一处。他家里租着马家三亩坡田，三亩地，一年的租子是收成的六成。马三去年跟他爹说过一句话：「你家小子跟着小宝，租子减一成。」这一成，他爹记在心上，他也记在心上。

发到一半，周衡搁下了笔，站起身来。周衡站着说话，一年里没有几回，执事房门口登时静了。他道：「还有一桩。秘境出来，腊月初八，外门大比。头名，赏筑基丹一枚。」队伍里「嗡」的一声。他等那嗡声落下去，又道：「一年一颗。今年，就这一颗。」说罢坐下，接着发灵石，好像方才说的是明天伙房吃萝卜。排在小满前头的孙二狗，捧着三块灵石，却不走，憋红了脸问：「周师兄，零……零层的，能上台么？」周衡道：「能。名册上有名字的，都能。」孙二狗「哦」了一声，又问：「上过么？」周衡翻了翻账簿：「三十年，没有。」孙二狗低着头走了，走了几步，摸了摸腰里那个布包，小声道：「……那我上一回。赢一场，写信告诉我娘。」

队伍后头，鲁泥鳅扯着嗓子接了一句：「大比的规矩，我爷爷都背得出——十七条。头十六条人人用，第十七条，三十年没人用过：头一轮输了的，一炷香里交十块灵石，还能再上去一回。」旁边的人哄地笑了：「一炷香里掏得出十块灵石的，还会输头一轮？」周衡头也不抬：「规矩在名录上，写着的。」

小满把「筑基丹」三个字在心里过了一遍——葛六说过，周衡也说过，那时候听着像是天上的事；这时候，天上的事到了执事房门口，离腊月初八，还有三十七天。

十步外，还是那张桌子，还是那只描金小木匣，匣上照旧贴着红纸，写着「公中」。马小宝坐在匣子后头，身后的跟班，今日由两个换成了三个，一个个抱着胳膊，站得跟门神一般。他听见「筑基丹」三个字，把手里的桂花糕咬了一口，慢悠悠地道：「今年的丹，姓马。」说完，拿指节笃笃地敲着木匣，眼皮也不抬：「沈小满。两块。」
story.en:
On the last night of the tenth month, just past the third watch, someone by the window of the long bunk in Chending Abbey's outer court sat bolt upright and shouted: "The water's gone!"

It was a shrill, urgent cry, and it woke more than half the room: some swore, some groped for their shoes, some trod on a neighbour's face. Xiaoman, on the bunk nearest the door, pulled his quilt round him and squeezed to the window. One look down the mountain and he froze. Under the moon, the Si had vanished. The broad river had shrunk to one bright thread in the middle of its bed, and on either side stretched mud flats white as far as the eye could see; in the bend below Mount Chending something black stood up out of the mud, square, more than ten feet high, like a door.

"The hidden realm," said the one who had woken them, and his voice shook. "The hidden realm is open." The notice had been on the board a day or two, and it said the first of the eleventh month; nobody had thought the river would go all at once, in the middle of the night.

Xiaoman lay back on his bunk, touched the token on his chest and whispered: "Yinyue, that cliff on the left — do you know it?" The token didn't answer. At the far end, on the best bunk by the brazier — crunch, crunch, one at a time, very slow, very even — Ma Xiaobao was eating osmanthus cake again. When he was done he balled up the oil paper and tossed it behind him onto the last bunk, and mumbled into the dark: "What's to fear. The ones who fall off cliffs are fools." Nobody answered him.

The last bunk stood under the draughty window, and in it slept a long thin senior everyone called Old Wilt. He was the son of one of the Ma family's tenants, three years in the gate, Qi Refining layer two, and he said maybe three sentences a day. He picked up the ball of oil paper, smoothed it out, folded it into a neat square and tucked it into his coat, to throw away for Ma Xiaobao first thing in the morning. On the night of the twelfth of the tenth month, in the woodshed, at the twentieth blow, the one of the five who had pulled his hand back and said, low, "Enough" — that was him. Ever since, Ma Xiaobao had made him sleep under the window.

On the first day of the eleventh month, before dawn, the usual long queue formed outside the stewards' office. Zhou Heng sat behind the elm table with the ledger thick as a pillow open before him, calling a name, handing out three stones, then fishing a bronze name tablet from an old wooden chest at his feet, the person's name cut on the back. His manner was not quite as usual today: with every handful he looked up and added, "In the hidden realm, keep your life first. Lose an herb, it grows back next year; lose a person, and the books don't balance." A new disciple asked him, "Brother Zhou, has anyone ever died in there?" Zhou Heng leafed through the ledger to the last few pages, yellower than the rest, where a few names stood with a red line under each. He looked at them a while, closed the book and said: "Keep your life first."

Right behind Xiaoman in the queue was Old Wilt. He took his three stones but didn't move; he stared at the closed ledger and asked, low: "Brother Zhou, the ones with the red stroke… do their families know?" Zhou Heng raised his eyes and looked at him. "The temple sends someone to tell them." Old Wilt nodded and tucked the three stones into his coat, beside the square of folded oil paper. His family rented three mu of hillside field from the Ma family — three mu, and the rent was six-tenths of the harvest. Last year Ma San had said one thing to his father: "Your boy follows Xiaobao, and the rent comes down a tenth." That tenth his father kept in his heart, and so did he.

Halfway through, Zhou Heng put down his brush and stood up. Zhou Heng seldom spoke standing, and the queue went quiet at once. "One more thing. After the hidden realm: the eighth of the twelfth month, the outer court contest. First place wins one Foundation pill." A hum ran down the line. He waited for it to settle, then said: "One a year. This year, this one." And he sat down and went on handing out stones, as if he'd said the kitchen would serve radish tomorrow. Sun Ergou, just ahead of Xiaoman, took his three stones but didn't move, and asked, red to the ears: "Brother Zhou, can… can someone at layer zero go up?" "Yes. Anyone on the register can." "Oh." Then: "Has anyone ever?" Zhou Heng leafed through the ledger: "Thirty years — no." Sun Ergou walked off with his head down; a few steps on he touched the cloth pouch at his waist and said softly, "…Then I'll go up once. Win one bout, and write and tell my ma."

From the back of the queue Lu the Loach called out: "My grandpa knows the contest rules by heart — seventeen of them. The first sixteen everyone uses. The seventeenth nobody's used in thirty years: lose your first round, pay ten spirit stones inside one stick of incense, and you get to go up once more." The people round him roared: "If you could turn out ten stones in one stick of incense, would you lose your first round?" Zhou Heng didn't look up: "The rule's in the register. It's written."

Xiaoman turned the words Foundation pill over in his mind — Ge Liu had said them, Zhou Heng had said them, and then they'd sounded like something in the sky; now the sky had come down to the stewards' door, and the eighth of the twelfth month was thirty-seven days off.

Ten steps on, the same table, the same little gilt box, the same red paper on it: COMMON FUND. Ma Xiaobao sat behind it; his followers had gone up from two to three today, arms folded, standing like door gods. At the words Foundation pill he bit his osmanthus cake and drawled, "This year's pill is named Ma." Then he rapped the box with a knuckle without lifting his eyelids: "Shen Xiaoman. Two."

exits.means: pays two stones to Ma Xiaobao's common fund

story.zh:
孙二狗在公中匣子前头，交的是一块。小满便道：「小宝哥，孙师兄交的是一块。」马小宝道：「他是他，你是你。」小满道：「那是为什么？」马小宝这才抬起眼皮，冲他咧嘴一笑：「因为你收了个畜生。畜生也要吃饭。」小满心想，小狰吃的是药园的残株，残株是周衡记在账上给他的，跟公中半文钱的干系也没有。可他没有说。他数出两块灵石，放进匣子里，道：「小宝哥说得对。畜生也要吃饭。」马小宝把那两块灵石捞起来，在手心里掂了一掂，没听出这话里有什么不对，很满意地挥了挥手。

小满往前走了十步，停下来，从怀里摸出那个红糖包纸订的小本子，舔了舔笔尖，写道：**冬月初一。公中。灵石两块。马小宝。因由：畜生也要吃饭。**写到「畜生」两个字，他笔尖停了一停，想了一想，没有写明是哪一个畜生。写完了，他摊开手掌。掌心里剩下一块灵石，灰扑扑的，只这一块。

执事房外头那片空场上，一早便摆开了七八张桌子，桌上铺着一张张发黄的纸，卖的是秘境的地图。十年前进去的人画一张，二十年前的画一张，三十年前的又是一张，互相抄，互相补，哪里的石板踩上去会翻，都标得清清楚楚。卖地图的是几个上一届的老弟子，小满认得其中两个——十月十二那天夜里，在柴房后头，一个踹的是他的左边肋骨，一个踹的是右边。原来公中的买卖，不止收灵石一样。

「一块灵石一张！不买地图进秘境，好比瞎子进山！」小满在桌前站住了，把那张地图从头看到尾。画得最密的是往右那一条路：一条长廊，三间石室，一座石桥，桥那头一片灵草园子，园子旁边注着一行小字：「此处灵草，三十年前尚有。」底下一行，是另一个人的笔迹：「二十年前，尚有三株。」再往下，墨迹最新：「十年前，无。」小满看到这里，心里便有了数。他爹教过他：鹿不走人走过的道。这张地图上画的，是三百年、几千个人走过的道，剩下的，只有一行一行越写越短的小字。

他把那块灵石攥在手心里，没有买。身后有人拍他肩膀，回头一看，是阿禾。她穿着那件大一号的灰袍，袖子挽了三道，鼻头冻得通红，手里捏着一张地图，比桌上卖的还要新，还要密。阿禾道：「你不买？」小满道：「一块灵石，买一张写着『无』的纸，不划算。」阿禾看了他一会儿，把地图塞给了他：「借你。」小满一愣：「那你呢？」阿禾面无表情地道：「我背下来了。他们卖一块，我借来看一夜，给了五十文——我说我只看一半。」小满道：「你看了多少？」阿禾道：「全看了。」

小满张着嘴，半天合不上。阿禾道：「五十文，记着。」她转身便走，走了两步，又回过头来，补了一句：「往右走。右边人多。人多，死不了。」
story.en:
At the common-fund box Sun Ergou paid one. "Brother Xiaobao," said Xiaoman, "Brother Sun paid one." "He's him and you're you." "Why's that?" Only then did Ma Xiaobao raise his eyelids and grin: "Because you took in a beast. Beasts have to eat too." Xiaoman thought: the little zheng ate the herb garden's culls, which Zhou Heng entered in his books for him — nothing to do with the common fund. But he didn't say so. He counted two stones into the box: "Brother Xiaobao is right. Beasts have to eat too." Ma Xiaobao scooped up the two stones and weighed them in his palm, heard nothing wrong in it, and waved him on, well pleased.

Ten steps on Xiaoman stopped, took out the little notebook sewn from red-sugar wrapping paper, licked his brush and wrote: **First of the eleventh month. Common fund. Two stones. Ma Xiaobao. Reason: beasts have to eat too.** At the word beasts his brush paused; he thought a moment and didn't write which beast he meant. Then he opened his hand. One stone left in his palm, dull grey, just the one.

On the open ground outside the stewards' office seven or eight tables had been set up since early morning, spread with yellowed sheets: maps of the hidden realm. The ones who went in ten years ago drew one, twenty years ago another, thirty years ago another, copying each other, filling each other in — which flagstone tipped when you stepped on it, all marked plain. The sellers were last year's seniors, and Xiaoman knew two of them: on the night of the twelfth of the tenth month, behind the woodshed, one had kicked his left ribs and the other his right. So the common fund's business wasn't only stones.

"One stone a map! Go in without one and you're a blind man in the hills!" Xiaoman stopped at a table and read a map end to end. The densest part was the road to the right: a corridor, three chambers, a stone bridge, and beyond it an herb garden with a small note: "Herbs here thirty years ago." Under it, in another hand: "Twenty years ago, three left." And under that, the newest ink: "Ten years ago, none." Xiaoman had seen enough. His father had taught him: deer don't walk where men walk. This map was a road three hundred years and thousands of people had walked, and all that was left of it was a line of notes getting shorter each time.

He closed his hand on the stone and didn't buy. Someone tapped his shoulder: A He, in her grey robe a size too big, sleeves rolled three times, nose red with cold, holding a map newer and denser than any on the tables. "You're not buying?" "One stone for a paper that says none — not worth it." She looked at him a while, then pushed her map into his hands: "Lend you." "Then what about you?" "I learned it by heart," she said, deadpan. "They sell it for one stone; I borrowed it for a night for fifty cash — I said I'd only read half." "How much did you read?" "All of it."

Xiaoman's mouth hung open. "Fifty cash," said A He. "On account." She turned to go, took two steps, looked back and added: "Go right. There's more people on the right. More people, nobody dies."

what.en: The first of the eleventh month, at the hidden realm's door: you didn't pay the common fund. He smiled: people die in the hidden realm all the time.

story.en:
Xiaoman closed his hand on his stones. "Brother Xiaobao, the common fund on the first is one."

Ma Xiaobao didn't lift his eyelids; he only rapped the box twice more with a knuckle and smiled: "In the hidden realm, people die now and then. Nothing strange in it."

Xiaoman didn't answer that. He walked off with his stones in his fist. Ten steps on he took out the little notebook sewn from red-sugar wrapping paper and wrote: **First day, eleventh month. Common fund. Not paid. Ma Xiaobao: in the hidden realm, people die now and then.**

On the open ground outside the stewards' office seven or eight tables had been set up since early morning, spread with yellowed sheets: maps of the hidden realm. The ones who went in ten years ago drew one, twenty years ago another, thirty years ago another, copying each other, filling each other in — which flagstone tipped when you stepped on it, all marked plain. The sellers were last year's seniors, and Xiaoman knew two of them: on the night of the twelfth of the tenth month, behind the woodshed, one had kicked his left ribs and the other his right. So the common fund's business wasn't only stones.

"One stone a map! Go in without one and you're a blind man in the hills!" Xiaoman stopped at a table and read a map end to end. The densest part was the road to the right: a corridor, three chambers, a stone bridge, and beyond it an herb garden with a small note: "Herbs here thirty years ago." Under it, in another hand: "Twenty years ago, three left." And under that, the newest ink: "Ten years ago, none." Xiaoman had seen enough. His father had taught him: deer don't walk where men walk. This map was a road three hundred years and thousands of people had walked, and all that was left of it was a line of notes getting shorter each time.

He closed his hand on the stone and didn't buy. Someone tapped his shoulder: A He, in her grey robe a size too big, sleeves rolled three times, nose red with cold, holding a map newer and denser than any on the tables. "You're not buying?" "One stone for a paper that says none — not worth it." She looked at him a while, then pushed her map into his hands: "Lend you." "Then what about you?" "I learned it by heart," she said, deadpan. "They sell it for one stone; I borrowed it for a night for fifty cash — I said I'd only read half." "How much did you read?" "All of it."

Xiaoman's mouth hung open. "Fifty cash," said A He. "On account." She turned to go, took two steps, looked back and added: "Go right. There's more people on the right. More people, nobody dies."
